title: Recruiter email templates to get more replies
summary: Common outreach mistakes lose you replies before candidates even open the email. Here are recruiter email templates by scenario that actually get read.
body_markdown:
Prospects don’t read past the subject line on the majority of emails recruiters send.


The failure rate has nothing to do with your writing style; it depends on how the message fits the candidate’s situation. Recruiting emails need the right mix of contextual priming and personalization to get read, and using a template can help.


This guide gives you recruiter email templates for specific hiring scenarios, so you can reach any type of candidate with a message that gets read. We'll also cover how to write a recruiting email and the common mistakes to avoid.


##


**What is a recruiting email template?**


A recruiting email template is a form of reusable outreach that recruiters can adjust to fit different hiring stages and scenarios.


Strong templates share a few common elements:


-


An enticing email subject line


-


Role context, in brief


-


A clear candidate value statement


-


A low-friction next step


##


**Common recruiting email mistakes**


Before building a template, recruiters should know the most common mistakes that lead candidates to avoid opening or replying to your emails.


###


**Delivery and candidate-experience mistakes**


-


**Vague subject lines:** Candidates open emails when subject lines tease interesting information or opportunities, express urgency, or a combination of the two. Those that don’t tend to get skipped.


-


**Wrong channels:** Reach out to candidates where they are. Sending the open job description to an old email the candidate rarely checks instead of their active LinkedIn account is a common mistake.


-


**Poor mobile readability:** Odds are good that candidates will check your message on their phone first. Make sure the content is suited for that experience.


-


**Incorrect details:** You only get one chance to make a first impression, and misspelling the candidate’s name or referencing an incorrect job title makes the wrong one.


###


**Messaging and follow-up email mistakes**


-


**Generic copy:** Candidates can tell when you swap their details into the same tired message you sent everyone else on your short list. The candidate’s time is valuable, so make sure your message reflects interest or cites an actual detail from their work. This is especially important when using a template, which encourages you to use recycled language. Personalize the message enough that it doesn’t look like boilerplate.


-


**Mistargeted outreach:** Pitching a mid-level role to a director, for example, wastes everyone’s time and potentially offends the candidate on the other end.


-


**Aggressive asks:** Strive to make the request easy enough for the candidate to say “yes” without second-guessing. Hopping in their inbox to ask for a resume and a 30-minute call in the first message does the opposite.


-


**One-and-done follow-up:** People get busy, and the candidate at the top of your shortlist is no different. Giving up after the first message means you risk losing the best candidates just because they weren’t aware of it in their inbox that day.


##


**How to write a recruiting email**


Effective recruitment emails all cover similar terrain, from a snappy subject line to content that proves you actually read and checked the candidate’s profile for role alignment before reaching out.


###


**Message elements that drive replies**


-


**Personalization:** Messages need to reflect, in one way or another, that you’ve taken the time to read up on the candidate in order to get a reply. Reference either a public project, recent LinkedIn post, or a career or educational stop you both have in common.


-


**Concise language:** Keep the message short enough to scan quickly while still including enough detail to ground the ask.


-


**Candidate-first value:** Solid candidates get a lot of inbound recruitment messages in their inbox. Make yours stand out by showing what they stand to gain from the role up front.


###


**Cadence and delivery rules**


The most important element is keeping a human in the loop to avoid outreach that comes off as overly robotic.


Specific things to watch include:


-


**Send timing:** Leave breathing room between every message of at least a few days, capping the total quantity of messages at 3 or 4.


-


**Stop conditions:** Build logic into the flow to prevent new messages when the candidate expresses disinterest.


-


**Handoff triggers:** When candidates reply positively, transition to human-led communication.


-


**Verified emails:** Sending to an outdated list generates bounces, and bounces can throw deliverability off for the entire team’s outreach. Make sure contact info is up to date.


-


**Unsubscribe language:** Always explicitly offer candidates the opportunity to unsubscribe from your list.


-


**Reply monitoring:** Set up the actual daily human monitoring to ensure nothing slips through the cracks.


##


**Recruiting email templates by scenario**


The below templates build on our existing[recruiting email template library](https://juicebox.ai/blog/recruiting-email-templates) . They work best when your[candidate sourcing strategies](https://juicebox.ai/blog/candidate-sourcing-strategies) and broader recruitment process successfully narrow down the shortlist of people who fit the role’s requirements.


###


**Outbound and sourced-candidate templates**


Personalize these using publicly available information gleaned from the candidate’s LinkedIn or other profiles.


####


**Cold email outreach**


**Subject line** : \[Role\] at \[company name\] and your work on \[publicly listed project\]


Hi \[first name\],


I saw your \[post, public talk, article, etc.\] on \[topic\], and it made me think of you for the \[role\] opening on our \[team or company name\]. We’re looking for somebody to \[quick scope description\]. Would you be open to a 15-minute chat this week to see if it’s worth a larger conversation?


Best regards,


\[Your name\]


####


**Sourced profile**


**Subject line** : \[Team\] is hiring for a \[name of role\] at \[company name\]


Hi \[name\],


Your move from \[previous company\] to \[current company\] demonstrates a strong interest in \[specific problem\]. We’re solving a version of it at \[company name\]. If a short intro sounds interesting, reply with a time, and I’ll send an invitation.


####


**Hard-to-fill technical role**


**Subject line:** \[Specific, technical problem\] at \[company name\]


Hi \[name\],


We’re hiring a \[role or job title\] to work on \[specific technical challenge\] at \[company name\]. Your work on \[public repo or paper\] is the closest match I’ve found. Would you be interested in having a quick intro call? I’d be happy to share the architecture and comp details upfront with the call invitation.


####


**Portfolio find**


**Subject line** : Your \[portfolio piece or work sample\] and a \[role\] at \[company name\]


Hi \[first name\],


I saw the \[work or project details\] in your portfolio, and it’s close to what our team does. We’re looking to fill a \[position at company\] opening with \[specific scope details\]. Happy to share the full picture on a quick call or answer some questions here if you’re interested.


###


**Referral, rediscovery, or follow-up templates**


####


**Referral**


**Subject line** : \[Referrer name\] suggested I reach out


Hi \[first name\],


\[Referrer\] on our team brought your name up when we opened a \[role\] search. They said \[specific reason for reaching out\]. Would you be open to a quick call to learn more?


####


**Past candidate or rediscovery in ATS**


**Subject line** : New \[role\] opening at \[company name\]


Hi \[first name\],


We connected in \[month, year\] over the \[job title\] role at \[company name\]. A \[role\] opening just came up that matches what you said you were looking for last time: \[detail or note from prior conversation\]. Would you be open to a fresh conversation?


####


**No-response follow-up**


**Subject line** : Re: \[original subject\]


Hi \[first name\],


Just bumping this in case it got buried. The \[role\] search is still open, and your background stands out. If the timing is off on your end, just let me know, and I’ll close the loop on this conversation.


###


**High-priority role variants**


For executive searches, get straight to the point. Open with the mandate and who the role reports to. For example, “We're hiring a VP of Engineering to lead a 40-person org through a platform rebuild, reporting directly to the CTO.”


For technical roles, lead with the technical details and the problem you’re solving. For example, We're building a real-time fraud detection system handling millions of transactions a day, and we need a senior backend engineer who's worked on low-latency, high-throughput infrastructure.


##


**How to tailor templates by audience**


Templates are the documents you build off of when opening a new campaign. But sometimes adjustments are also necessary. Before hitting send, make sure they reflect factors like the stage of the relationship, how warmed up the candidate is, and the source.


###


**Tailoring by audience and funnel-stage**


Here’s how to make adjustments based on the target audience or funnel considerations:


-


**Passive prospects:** When[sourcing passive candidates](https://blog.juicebox.ai/blog/sourcing-passive-candidates) , focus your approach on their published work or projects. Remove the commitment barrier by making the ask simple, and expect to follow up a few times before breaking through.


-


**Referral prospects:** Open with the referrer's name and the reason you’re reaching out. This approach often hinges on the quality of your prospect's relationship with the referrer, so make sure it’s a solid connection.


-


**Past applicants:** These prospects still have a rejection email from your company somewhere in their inbox. So, don’t gloss over the previous application cycle and act like it never happened. Name it, say what changed, and remove as much friction as possible from the next step.


-


**Reconnects:** Drop some breadcrumbs from the last conversation, and be clear on what’s different now.


-


**Executive, technical, or evergreen hiring** : Focus on what each most wants to know about the opportunity. For execs, that’s mandate, scope, and who they report to. Engineers want the technical background and stack details, and evergreen candidates want to know why you should stay in touch when there’s no active opportunity on the table.


###


**Channel signals and personalization boundaries**


There’s a fine line between doing your due diligence on a candidate and referencing a highly personal deep cut from their life that scares them off, and you don’t want to be the recruiter who crosses the line.


The easiest way to toe the line: Focusing on public professional channels. For practical purposes, this means LinkedIn information, GitHub repo activity, a public portfolio, or any context you’ve previously pulled from a referral source or the information you’ve gathered from the ATS.
